title: Sigma0 26.5 oxygen loss moved east across the North Pacific from about 1990 at 170-180 W to 2001 at CalCOFI; layer thinning explains 0-50% (WOD ship data 1950-2025)
abstract: Question: was the sigma0 26.5 oxygen low off southern California (CalCOFI) a local event, did the loss start at the same time everywhere, and does a tracer-free ventilation index (thickness of the 26.4-26.6 class) explain it? Approach: we used all World Ocean Database bottle and CTD casts with oxygen (26,019 casts, 1,738 cruises, 1950-2025) and 150,255 Argo temperature-salinity profiles in 15-50 N, 120-180 W. We fitted regional fixed-effects year series, epoch changes with a cruise bootstrap, ramp-model onset years, a thickness test (fit 1950-1996, test 1997-2025) and lagged forecasts of the CalCOFI index (fit 1950-2006, test 2007-2025). Results: from 1984-1996 to 2009-2025, oxygen fell by 20-38 umol/kg in every 10-degree band at 28-42 N from 180 W to the coast, and by 34.5 umol/kg in the transition zone; in 1950-1983 offshore oxygen was within 2 umol/kg of the 1984-1996 level. The midpoint of the decline was near 1992-1993 at 160-180 W, 1995 at 130-150 W, 1998 at 125-130 W and 2002 in the CalCOFI band. It moved east by 0.11 yr per degree (0.00 to 0.33; 97% of draws positive), about 2 cm/s, and it was later in water with higher reference AOU (0.12 yr per umol/kg, 0.08 to 0.20). This order does not agree with a simultaneous change of local respiration. The 26.4-26.6 layer thinned by 13-17 m only west of 150 W and by 11 m in the gyre, at about the same time as the oxygen loss there. Thinning explains 20-50% of the loss where it occurred and 0-6% in the transition zone and the California Current. No lagged upstream series forecast the 2007-2025 CalCOFI low better than persistence (RMSE 4.3 or more against 3.7). Argo oxygen in WOD was 10 umol/kg low at 56 float-ship crossovers and was not used. Limitations: only 3-7 offshore ship cruises with oxygen in 2009-2025, no inter-cruise oxygen calibration, wide onset intervals, design choices after a first look at part of the data, and timing that cannot separate less ventilation from more respiration or lower preformed oxygen upstream.

citations.reason: We use its CalCOFI annual sigma0 26.5 oxygen index as the forecast and timing target, and its forecast-test design.

We reuse its regions and GLODAP isopycnal code. With all WOD ship data we support an offshore source of the loss, but no lagged upstream series forecasts CalCOFI and the timing does not fix a 10-year transit time.
We apply its class-thickness ventilation test to the northeast Pacific; there thickness explains 0-50% of the loss.
